step.title: Decide
step.question: Am I ready for this option?
tagline: You know what you want, and you have found a place where it could work.
intro: Now comes the question most people rush or avoid: am I ready for this option?

In this step, you test your plan before you commit to it. You check five green lights: money, papers, people, place and your Plan B. You consider what could go wrong and the order of operations. Then you decide: go, not yet, or no.

All three answers are good ones. A clear "not yet", with the conditions written down, is worth more than a "go" that rests on hope. And a "no" you reach now costs far less than one you reach after you have sold your home.
Every exercise starts with a short explanation, then asks you to apply it to your own life.

what_you_need.title: What you need before you start
bullets: Your Working Direction and Life Picture from Step 1, including your must-haves and dealbreakers.
Your Explore Summary from Step 2: the place you want to plan for, and what you still do not know about it.
Your updated money picture, with the real costs you created in Step 2.
what_you_need.after: If you have not completed Step 2, you can still work through this step, but many answers will rest on guesses. Mark them as estimates, and go back to Step 2 before you make the final decision.

how_it_works.title: How this step works
bullets: This step is about testing. You check your plan against real numbers, real rules and real people.
Each green light gets a colour. Green means ready. Amber means not ready yet, but you know what to do. Red means something stops this option as it stands.
Amber is normal. Most people finish this step with a few ambers. What matters is that each one has a next action and a date.
This step stays high-level. Modules that go deeper are planned for later and are not part of this course, such as Portugal in detail, Your Money Plan and starting a company.
Some questions are expert work. Tax, residence law and contracts depend on your situation. This workbook helps you prepare your questions. The answers come from qualified professionals.
Each part ends with "What does this tell me?" Use your answers to complete a summary.
Each light has an "If you are staying" box. It shows what the check means for a change where you live.
The people in the examples are made up. They show what an answer can look like. Your answers can be completely different.

word_help.title: Word help
items: not ready yet, with a clear next action.
this blocks the option as it stands.
a step you can reverse at low cost, such as renting.
a step that is expensive or impossible to reverse, such as selling your home.
what you will do if the plan does not work, decided before you need it.
income you have evidence will continue in your new situation.
how sure you are about a number or fact, as in Steps 1 and 2.

tips: Part 1 takes the most time because some lights need a phone call, an adviser or a conversation at home. Spread it over two or three weeks.

route.title: Your route through Step 3
rows: Bring your work together and name the decision
Put things in the right order
Only if you stay: plan your change where you are

step.staying: Staying and changing your life where you are? This step is for you too. The option you test can also be a change where you live: working four days a week, a new job, your own business, more space, or another region in your own country. Test it in Parts 1 to 4, just like a move. You can skip 1.2 Papers and 1.4 Place unless your change involves them, for example, moving to another region or renovating. Then finish with "Your staying route" at the end of this step.

parts.label: Start
parts.title: The decision on the table
parts.promise: A clear decision starts with a clear question.
intro: "Should I move to Portugal?" sounds like one question. It is usually several. Move for good, or for a trial year? Rent first, or buy? This year, or in two years? On your own, or with your family? If the question is vague, the answer will be vague too.

Write the decision down as precisely as you can. Include what "go" would mean, and when you want to decide. Then you know exactly what you are testing in the rest of this step. The same goes for staying. Name the exact change you are testing.
parts.route_title: Bring your work together and name the decision

finish.title: My Decision Question
finish.description: The exact decision you are testing in this step.

exercises.title: The decision on the table

fields.label: Bring your work with you
fields.hint: Copy the most important lines from Steps 1 and 2. You will use them in every part of this step, and this workbook then holds your whole decision in one place.

fields.label: My life picture in three sentences (Step 1)
My must-haves (Step 1)
My dealbreakers (Step 1)
The place I want to go further with (Step 2)
What is still unknown about it (Step 2)

My confirmed income there, per month

rows: Keep them side by side. Fill in this page, the five green lights and both money checks once for each place. Then decide per place: go, not yet or no. The stress test in Part 2 and the final check in Part 4 help you choose between them.

example.text: Option: move to the Silver Coast with our two children. "Go" means renting for one year first, then deciding whether to buy. When: next summer, at the start of the school year. We decide together; the children get a say, but not a vote. Decide by: 31 March. If "not yet" or "no": we both try a four-day week and spend a long summer in Portugal each year.

tips: A trial year is a real option. Renting for a year, keeping your home, and keeping your work options open lets you test life before you commit. It costs more in the short term, but it can save you a great deal later.

parts.result: My Decision Question — the exact decision you are testing in this step.

parts.label: Part 1
parts.title: Five green lights
parts.promise: Five checks. Each one green, amber or red.
parts.intro_title: Why five lights, and not one feeling
intro: It is easy to feel ready before checking the practical details. Feelings matter, and you tested yours in Step 2. But a feeling cannot tell you whether your savings will last, whether your papers are in order, or whether your partner is really on board.

The five green lights split the decision into parts you can check: money, papers, people, place and your Plan B. You do not need five greens to start preparing. You need to know which lights are amber, and what will turn them green.

finish.title: My Green Lights
finish.description: Five checks, each with a colour, a next action and a date.

exercises.title: Money
exercises.kicker: Can you afford the change, and the life after it?
intro: In Step 1 you made a first money picture. In Step 2 you replaced guesses with real costs. Now you turn those numbers into a decision: does the money carry this plan, and for how long?

Look at three things. The one-time cost of the move. The monthly cost of your new life, compared with the income you can count on. And your reserve: money you keep aside, so one bad month or a delay does not end the plan.

Only confirmed income counts: income you have evidence will continue in your new situation. Agreed income gets its own line, with the month it starts, but it does not go into the check yet. Hoped-for income stays out, as in Step 1.

start_here.prompt: Check one: can your savings carry the change itself? Include the cost of deciding: viewing trips, advisers, translations, a second visit, and paying rent in two places for a while. People budget the move and forget the deciding.

row_labels: Savings I can use within a month
Minus: the cost of deciding
Minus: the one-time cost of the move
Minus: deposits, money I pay now and may only get back much later
Minus: my reserve
Minus: my return fund (from Plan B, kept apart)
Savings left to live on

fields.hint: Check two: does your confirmed income cover the month? Mark every cost known, estimated, or unknown. An unknown means the check is not finished yet.
row_labels: My confirmed income per month in the new place
Agreed income, and the month it starts (not counted yet)
My costs per month in the new place (known / estimate / unknown)
Left over or short each month
If short: how many months my savings left to live on can cover (my runway)
The runway I want, in months (my choice)
If everything costs 30% more: what changes?

fields.hint: Some money questions are expert work. Write down what you want to ask a tax adviser, ideally one who knows both countries.

fields.label: My money light
What would turn it green, and by when

bullets: Where will I be tax resident, and from when?
What happens to my income, pension or company when I move?
What happens to tax when I sell my home, or to my savings and investments?
Are there special tax rules for newcomers, and do they apply to me? These rules change often.

exercises.intro_after: If your confirmed income already covers your monthly costs, write "covered" as your runway. One thing still applies: your savings must still carry the move, your reserve and your return fund.
exercises.closing: Green means: check one is above zero, including the cost of deciding and your reserve, and your runway, counting confirmed income only, is at least the number of months you chose, or your confirmed income covers the month.
tips: Your reserve is yours to decide. A common way to think about it is how many months of costs you want covered if everything stopped. The amounts in the examples are made up to show how the check works.

example.text: Check one: savings €56,000, minus €3,000 for deciding (two trips, a lawyer, translations), €8,000 for the move, €3,000 in deposits and a €12,000 reserve (about four months of costs) and a €7,000 return fund, kept apart for Plan B. Left to live on: €23,000. Check two: confirmed income €2,400 from Ben's remote contract. Agreed: €900 a month for Lotte from October, not counted yet. Costs: €2,900 a month; rent is known, school costs are an estimate. Short: €500 a month, so the runway is 46 months. The runway we want: 12 months. If everything costs 30% more, we are €1,370 short, and the runway drops to about 17 months, still above what we want. Our light: amber, until Lotte's income is confirmed.

story.text: Before I moved, I made sure I had twelve months of living costs saved. I explained why in Step 1. I learned that structure matters as much as savings. In my first year in Portugal, I set up a Portuguese company with an accountant's help. I use it for my consultancy work, and later for the farm and rural tourism I have in mind. It also made sense given the land and renovation costs. That was the right choice for me, after advice. Your situation may be completely different, which is exactly why this is a question for an adviser, not for a forum.

exercises.expert_work: Tax rules for newcomers change often, and the right answer depends on your income, your assets and both countries involved. Talk to a qualified tax adviser before you move money, sell property, set up a company or change where you pay tax.
exercises.staying: Use the same two checks for your change. Check one: can your savings carry the change itself, such as a course, an income gap or a renovation? Check two: does your confirmed income cover the month after the change, for example, on four days a week, or in the first year of your own business? Leave out the lines about moving.

exercises.title: Papers
exercises.kicker: Can you legally live there, and do you have the basics in place?
intro: Paperwork takes time, and some steps depend on others. Many of them can start before you move.
In Step 2, you checked whether you are allowed to live in the country. Here you list everything you will need, in which order, and how long each step takes.

start_here.prompt: Tick what applies to you. For each item, write whether it is done, in progress or not started, and how long it takes.

row_labels: Tax number (in Portugal: NIF)
A bank account that works for payments there
Right to live there: visa, residence permit or EU registration.
Proof of address
Health cover: public registration and private insurance
Social security (if you work or run a business)
Driving licence: still valid, or to be exchanged
School places for children
Travel papers for pets
Deregistering at home: tax, health, address

columns.label: Done, in progress or not started

fields.label: My papers light
What would turn it green, and by when

exercises.closing: Green means: you have confirmed your own route on the official page and written down the date you checked it, you have the full list of documents, and you know the order and how long each step takes.
where_to_check: For Portugal, two different routes exist, and people mix them up. With an EU, EEA, Andorran or Swiss passport, you can live there and register at the câmara municipal for a registration certificate (see aima.gov.pt). With any other passport, you normally need a visa before you travel (vistos.mne.gov.pt), and then apply for a residence permit with AIMA. For everyone: you can request a tax number (NIF) through the Portal das Finanças or gov.pt, also from abroad; your health service user number (número de utente) comes through your local health centre (gov.pt, sns.gov.pt); for driving licences, see imt-ip.pt. Checked 28 September 2026.
tips: Do things in the right order. Some steps depend on others. In Portugal, you usually get a tax number first because you need it for a bank account, a rental contract, or a purchase.

story.text: I started before I moved. I arranged my Portuguese tax number through an online service and made sure I had a bank account that supported international payments. You need both to buy land. With the help of an agent, who checked the essential land papers, and a lawyer, I signed the promissory contract about two months after I decided to purchase the land. I signed the deed at the notary about three months later. Registering the sale then took only about a month. That winter, the parish council (junta de freguesia) confirmed my address, and the câmara municipal issued my EU registration certificate. My tax number was first registered to my Bali address, so I changed that as well. Early the next year, I set up my company with an accountant, who also helped me get my social security numbers and Portuguese bank accounts. My health insurance came a few months later, followed by my public health service number.

exercises.staying: This light is usually short. Think of your employment contract and notice period, permission from your employer for fewer hours or remote work, registering a business, or a permit if you renovate or build. If your change needs none of this, mark this light green and move on.

exercises.title: People
exercises.kicker: Who comes with you, who stays behind, and who will be there?
intro: A move changes more lives than your own. A partner who agrees at the kitchen table can feel very different in the first wet winter. Children, parents, and close friends shape the decision, even when they aren't moving.

There's another side to this light: the people you will have there. In a new place, you start without the network you built over the years. Who will you call when the car breaks down, when you need a doctor, or when you get bad news?

Each person who moves with you fills in their own page first, before you talk together, as in Steps 1 and 2. Involve children the way you normally involve them in big decisions. Every family does this differently. Some parents decide first and then explain; others let teenagers help choose the place or the school. Whatever you choose, tell them early, and be honest about what will change and what will stay the same.

columns.label: What this move means for them
What they need to say yes

fields.hint: Now the second question: who will be there for you in the first year? Write down the people or groups you already know there, and how you will meet more.

fields.label: My people light
What would turn it green, and by when

exercises.closing: Green means: everyone the move or change affects has done their own thinking, you have talked it through together, and what each person needs to say yes is in place or planned.
exercises.talk: Ask your partner, or the person closest to you, three questions. What are you most looking forward to? What worries you most? What would make you want to go back? Listen first, and write their answers down in their own words.

story.text: I went through the whole process on my own, and that is one reason this Blueprint exists. But I was not alone for long. The owners who sold me the land and I clicked from day one, and they have helped me with many things. The English couple whose Airbnb I stayed in made the same move years earlier; he gave me my accountant's contact. In my first months in Portugal, I lost my mother. When she was ill, the life I had built gave me the freedom to fly back and spend real time with her. When I lost her, these new friends, together with my closest friend, carried me through. Today they are family.

exercises.staying: A change where you live affects people too: your partner, your children, your colleagues and your friends. Fill in the same table for everyone your change touches. The first-year question becomes: Who supports you while you make the change?

exercises.title: Place
exercises.kicker: Does the place still fit, now that you know it better?
intro: In Step 2 you researched your place and tested it with your own eyes. This light asks a harder question: are you sure enough to commit, and to what? A place you visited for two weeks is not yet a place you know.

The bigger the commitment, the more certain you need to be. Renting for a year asks for less certainty than buying. Buying land to build on asks for more certainty than buying a finished house. Match the step to what you know.

fields.label: The place I am deciding on
What is known about it
What is still an estimate or unknown
Have I seen it outside the high season? When?
Rent first or buy, and why
What would make me change my mind about this place?
My place light
What would turn it green, and by when

exercises.closing: Green means: the place still meets your must-haves after your test visit, you have seen it outside the high season, and what you commit to, renting or buying, matches what you know.
tips: Rent first if you can. A year in a rented home shows you the winters, the neighbours and the drive to the hospital before you own anything. If you want to buy, you can look for the right property while you live there.

Every câmara follows the same national rules, but they do not all read them the same way. One câmara may be open to new projects, while the next is stricter. Before you buy, try to meet the person who will handle your plans, share your ideas, and listen. At the very least, find out how that câmara (or the municipality in your chosen county) usually works. It can make the difference between a smooth process and many rounds of changes.

story.text: I did it the other way round. I bought before I moved, so renting to test the area wasn't part of my plan. I would still recommend it to most people. What gave me confidence was that the plot came with a renovation project for the ruin that the previous owners had already had approved. In Portugal, getting a project approved can easily take two years. It was one of the main reasons I chose this plot. Once the project was transferred to my name and I had chosen a contractor, I received the building permit. My design differed from theirs in places, but after a conversation with the câmara, we could start. One thing I would do differently: I only checked my other plans later. About half a year after I moved, I submitted a request for prior information (pedido de informação prévia, PIP) for a storage room, a garage and a few cabins for rural tourism. New-build cabins turned out to be impossible because of the Serra da Estrela nature park rules. My plans had changed by then, so it did not hurt much. But if you have specific plans for a property, ask for a PIP before the deed, if the owner agrees, and make the promissory contract say you can step out if the answer is no.

exercises.staying: Staying in your home? Skip this light, or mark it green. If your change involves your place, such as another region in your own country, more space or a renovation, use the same questions.

exercises.title: Plan B
exercises.kicker: What will you do if it does not work out?
intro: Nobody moves with a plan to fail. That's why you need to write down your Plan B now, while you are calm, not later, when you are tired, disappointed, or short on money.

A Plan B looks different for everyone. Some people trust themselves to rebuild and need very little. Others need much more security before they feel comfortable. It also depends on who moves with you and your situation: if you need to sell your house to pay for your new life, renting it out isn't an option. So first work out how much of a Plan B you need to feel comfortable. Then write down what fits you. A Plan B usually covers three things. What you keep, so going back or moving on stays possible: savings, a reserve, a way to earn. What would tell you it is not working: a warning sign, a number or a date. And what you would do then: go back, try another region, rent instead of own, or move on.

fields.label: How much of a Plan B I need to feel comfortable, and why
What I keep so that I can change course
My return fund: money to come back or move on, a first month somewhere, and where I would stay
The warning sign that tells me it is not working
The date or number when I look at it seriously
What I would do then
Who would help me
My Plan B light
What would turn it green, and by when

exercises.closing: Green means: your Plan B is written down at a level that makes you comfortable, with at least a warning sign, a review date and the first thing you would do.

example.text: Keep: we rent out our house for the first year instead of selling it. Return fund: €7,000, on top of our reserve and already deducted in our money check, for the move back, a first month in a holiday rental and storage; we could stay with my sister. Warning sign: the children are still unhappy at school after two terms, or we have used more than half of our reserve. Review date: 1 April next year. What then: return to our own house, or move to a different area in Portugal closer to an international school. Help: my sister and the parents we meet through the school.

story.text: I didn't write down a detailed Plan B, but I kept a way back. Part of it was financial: I set aside enough money that, if it didn't work out, I could decide what to do next in the moment, whether that meant renting, travelling, or moving to another country. And I kept Bali open. My company and bank accounts there stayed in place; I could easily apply for a new residence permit. In addition, my plan B was my experience. When I came back to the Netherlands from Thailand, I had nothing. I slept at my aunt's for the first few months, until I found an apartment and a job. Then I built a life in Bali, and then in Portugal. I knew I could always rebuild my life. I also trusted the signs on my path, and that has always worked out for me. That was enough for me, but a Plan B looks different for everyone. Write yours down in a way that makes you feel comfortable. You may never need it, and that is the best outcome.

exercises.staying: What if the change does not work? For example: can you go back to five days, return to a job, or keep one client while you build your business? The same rule applies: write down as much Plan B as you need to feel comfortable.

rows: Ready. It is known, not an estimate, and you have evidence.
Not ready yet, but you know what is missing. Write down the next action and a date.
This blocks the option as it stands. Change the option or the timing, or let it go.

parts.label: Part 2
parts.title: Stress-test your plan
parts.promise: A plan that only works on good days is not ready yet.
parts.intro_title: Why we look at the difficult days
intro: Imagining the good day is easy. The difficult day is where the information is. Winter, illness, a quiet week with nobody around, work that goes wrong: those days happen in every life, in every country. The question is not whether they come. It is whether you could manage them in the life you are building.

finish.title: My Risks
finish.description: Your biggest risks, the signs to watch, and what you will do.

exercises.title: Two futures
intro: An option you cannot imagine on a bad day is one you haven't really considered. So you picture both: an ordinary good day and an ordinary difficult day, five years from now.

start_here.prompt: Take the option you are deciding on and, if you have one, your best alternative. Staying? Compare your change with keeping things as they are. Imagine it is five years from now. For each option, write a normal good day and a normal difficult day.

fields.label: Option 1, a good day
Option 1, a difficult day
Option 2, a good day
Option 2, a difficult day

exercises.intro_after: In each day, notice who decides your time. Are your days busy by choice, or because others decide? And when do the busy transition years end: the paperwork, the renovation, finding work? More control over your time often comes after them, not straight away.

go_deeper.prompt: What would still be difficult, even after moving? Some things change with a place. Some things come with you.

story.text: After three years in Bali, the island no longer felt the same. Then I had an accident with my motorbike. It wasn't my fault, but they blamed me. It made me realise that, after all those years, they still saw me as a foreigner. When I found the self-sufficient life I wanted on YouTube, I saw two futures: staying in a place that no longer felt like home, or starting again somewhere that fitted my new picture. The hardest part was leaving the life and the friends I had built over three years, knowing I had to start again. But I knew it was the right decision.

exercises.title: What could go wrong?
intro: Fear is normal. Writing a fear down turns it into something you can work with. A fear in your head has no size. It is simply there, usually at three in the morning, and it makes every option feel dangerous. On paper, a fear gets four parts, and each part gives you something to do.

rows: Low, medium or high, or not sure. Some fears are real risks. Others are very unlikely, and naming that is a relief.
Would it cost you a weekend, or your savings? Small and likely is annoying. Big and likely needs a plan. If the impact would be serious, prepare a fallback even when you think it is unlikely.
What would you notice first, while there is still time to act? This is the most useful column.
Prevent it, reduce it, or prepare a fallback. Many fears shrink once you have one.

start_here.prompt: Check the risks of the option you are deciding on, and of your best alternative. Otherwise, you end up comparing one option's difficulties with the other option's best case.

go_deeper.prompt: Look at your biggest fear. What is it telling you? Maybe you need more information. Maybe two of your needs pull in different directions. Maybe it is a real risk to plan for.

example.text: Fear: my bakery fails in the first year. Likely: medium. Impact: big; I would lose savings. Warning sign: after six months, less than half the sales I need. What I can do: first sell at a local market for six months, set aside six months of costs, and know I can work for a bakery again.

summary.intro: Read through your answers, then use these questions to complete the summary below:

Which early warning signs will I watch?
What would still be difficult, wherever I live?

parts.label: Part 3
parts.title: Put things in the right order
parts.promise: Easy to undo first. Hard to undo last.
intro: The most expensive mistakes in a move are often not wrong choices. They are right choices made in the wrong order: selling the house before the papers are clear, signing a contract before the money is in place, or arriving before there is somewhere to live.

Do the steps you can undo cheaply first: a tax number, a bank account, a conversation with an adviser, renting, a trial period. Do the steps that are expensive or impossible to undo last: selling your home, resigning from your job, signing a purchase contract. And before each big step, write down what must be true first.
Staying? The same rule works. Talk to your employer before you hand in your notice, test your business idea before you invest in it, and rent extra space before you buy it.
parts.route_title: Put things in the right order

finish.title: My First Timeline
finish.description: The right steps, in the right order.

exercises.title: The right steps, in the right order

start_here.prompt: Some dates are not yours to choose, and they often decide the order. Write them down first.

row_labels: Start of the school year
Notice period for my job

fields.hint: List the main steps of your move. For each one, write whether it is easy or hard to undo, what must be true first, and roughly when you would take it.

example.text: Tax numbers and a bank account: easy to undo; now. Rent a house for a year: fairly easy; first, confirmed school places; February. Rent out our own house: fairly easy; first, a signed rental contract in Portugal; May. Lotte hands in her notice at her current job: hard; first, her new Portuguese income confirmed in a signed contract, and Ben's employer confirming in writing that his remote contract continues from Portugal; June. Buy a house: hardest; first, one full winter there and a green light on money; not before next year.

story.text: My own order was not the textbook one. I sold my house in Bali a couple of months before I visited Portugal. I spent two months travelling through Portugal. That same summer, I returned for a longer stay in an Airbnb close to the land and signed the promissory contract about two months after my trip. About three months later, I signed the deed. That autumn and winter, I travelled between Portugal, the Netherlands, and Bali: to be with my family, start the paperwork, and wrap up my life in Bali. The next spring, I came back for good. I stayed in the Airbnb again. A contractor started renovating the ruin, and soon after, I moved onto the land. About eight months later, just before Christmas, I moved into the house. That speed came from the approved project, the right contractor, my experience, and being on site every day. Selling first worked for me because my picture was very clear. I knew Bali was no longer my place, and my research showed me I wanted this life in Portugal. I also had a reserve, and I had done this before. If this is your first move, I would take the easy-to-undo steps first.

tips: Build in extra time. Papers, contractors and sales often take much longer than planned. Add a few months to every step you don't control.

parts.label: Part 4
parts.title: Make your decision
parts.promise: Go, not yet, or no. All three are real results.
intro: You have checked the five lights, looked at the difficult days and put the steps in order. Now you decide. Not forever: for now, with what you know.

Three rules help. Decide on paper first, then sleep on it for at least 48 hours before you tell anyone outside the decision. Decide together with the people it affects, after each of you has done your own thinking. And give every answer a date: when you start, when you review, or when you look at the question again.
parts.talk: Tell the people close to you what you decided, and why. Not to ask for permission, but so they can support you and you can say your decision out loud.

finish.title: My Decision
finish.description: Go, not yet, or no, with your reasons, conditions and dates.

exercises.title: One last check: must-haves and dealbreakers
intro: In Step 1 you named what your new life needs and what you will not accept. Hold this option against them one last time. It is the cheapest red light there is: a broken dealbreaker ends this option, whatever the other lights say.

exercises.title: My Decision

fields.label: My decision question (from the Start)
My decision
options: Go and change where I am

fields.label: Must-haves met, and no dealbreakers broken?
Why: my three main reasons
My lights: which are green, which are amber, and which are red
Conditions that must be true before the big steps
Who decided with me, and do we agree?
My first step
Date of my first step
When will I review this decision?
What would make me change it?

exercises.choice_explanations_intro: For "My decision", four answers are possible, and all four are good:
choice_explanations: Go. No light is red, and every amber light has a named condition, an action and a date. A go with conditions means you start preparing (Step 4, Prepare, is coming soon), but you take no hard-to-undo step until those conditions are met.
Go, and change where I am. Your option was a change where you live, and it passed the same test. Continue with "Your staying route" at the end of this step.

Not yet. The picture is right, but the conditions are not. Write down exactly what must change, and when you will look again. A "not yet" with a date is a decision. Without a date, it is a way of putting it off.
No. This option does not fit, or not at this price. That is a result, not a failure. Go back to Step 2 to look at another place, test a change where you live, or keep the life you have.

example.text: A completed page. Lotte and Ben are made up. Every line is filled in, including the conditions and the dates. Decision question: do we move to the Silver Coast with our two children, renting for a trial year from next summer? Decision: go, as a trial year, with conditions. We start preparing now; we sign nothing hard to undo until the conditions below are met. Must-haves: not all yet. All must-haves are met except one: a good school, which is an estimate until we visit and have places. That is a condition below. No dealbreakers broken. Why: our ordinary days there look like our Life Picture. The money lasts about 17 months even if everything costs 30% more, with our reserve and return fund untouched. The children are curious, not against it. Lights: green: papers and place. Amber: money, until Lotte's income is confirmed; people, until care for Ben's mother is arranged; Plan B, until a tenant has signed for our house. Red: none. Conditions: Lotte's income confirmed. Care for Ben's mother arranged. A tenant signed for our house. School places confirmed. Who decided: both of us, after each of us filled in our own page. The children were heard. We agree. First step: meet two care providers for Ben's mother. Date of my first step: before 15 March. Review: 1 April next year, whatever has happened by then. What would change it: no school places by May, or Lotte's income not confirmed by June: then we move the trial year back by one year.

parts.label: Staying route
parts.title: Your staying route
parts.promise: Build the life you want where you are.
parts.intro_title: Why staying needs a plan too
intro: Staying can be the best result of this Blueprint. But staying and changing nothing is not the same as building the life you want where you are. A change at home needs the same care as a move: a date, an order, money that works, people on board, and a way to check that it helps.

This part turns your decision into a plan. It is shorter than the moving steps, because you keep your home, your papers and your surroundings. What changes is how you use them. Use this part if your decision was "go and change where I am". Moving? Skip it and continue with Step 4.
parts.route_title: Only if you stay: plan your change where you are
parts.can_skip: Only if you are staying. If your decision was to move, skip this part and continue with Step 4.

finish.title: My Change Plan
finish.description: Your change where you are, with a date, a first step and a check-in.

start_here.prompt: Pick the date your change should be in place. Then count back: what has to happen first, and how long does it take? Think of a conversation with your employer, a notice period, a course, your first clients, or saving a buffer.

example.text: Change: four days a week from 1 March, with Fridays for my ceramics studio. Steps: talk to my manager in October; try a ceramics course in November to test the idea; review our budget with my partner in December; submit a formal request for four days in January, with two months' notice; my first Friday in the studio on 3 March.

start_here.prompt: In Part 1 you checked whether the money carries your change. Now make it concrete: what changes in your income, and from when? Which costs start or stop? And which conversation do you need to have first?

tips: Working fewer hours or starting a business can change your tax, your pension and your social security. Ask your employer, your pension fund or an adviser before you sign anything.

start_here.prompt: Your home and your week are where a change becomes real. In Step 1 you sorted your week into time fixed by others, must-dos and your own choice. Look at it again: what moves to "my choice" after this change?

fields.label: Who I tell, and when
What I need from my partner or family

start_here.prompt: The people around you notice a change at home as much as a move. Tell them what you are changing, why, and what you need from them. Some will cheer you on, and some will not understand. Look for people who already live the way you want to: they are your best source of advice.

fields.label: The first thing I do in week one
What I want to be true after 30 days

start_here.prompt: The first months decide whether a change sticks. Old habits pull you back, and work fills the free time again. Plan your first 90 days on purpose.

bullets: Do my ordinary days look more like my Life Picture than before?

start_here.prompt: Put two dates in your calendar: three months and one year after the change. On those dates, read your Life Picture from Step 1 again, and ask yourself three questions:

exercises.closing: If the answer disappoints you, you have not failed. You have learned what does not work, and that is the start of your next plan. And if the change works and you still want more, look at Step 2 again. Maybe your next step is a move after all.

parts.talk: Ask the person closest to you two questions. What do you think will change for you? And what do you need from me?

closing.title: What comes next
closing.intro: You have tested your plan against real numbers, real rules and real people, and you have made a decision. From here, the road splits: Step 4 if you move, and the staying route if you build the life you want where you are.
bullets: Going? Step 4, Prepare, is coming soon. It will turn your decision into a moving plan: what to arrange, in which order, and by when. Until then, your First Timeline from Part 3 is your plan.
Not yet? Work on your ambers, and revisit the date you set.
Staying and changing your life where you are? Your staying route, on the previous pages, completes your Blueprint. Keep your check-in dates.
No? Go back to Step 2 with what you have learned, or keep the life you have.
tips: Keep this workbook close. When doubt comes, and it will, read your reasons again. You made this decision with a clear head.
final: You will never be completely sure.
But you can be ready enough and know what to do next.
